issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in this profile. With assault trauma, the other trigger items (related sounds, being naked) plausibly cue danger/vulnerability, and the threat items are about danger and vigilance. Praise/positive attention points in a very different interpersonal direction and is not supported by corresponding appraisals or threat content, so it weakens cross-node coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'Fear going crazy' is poorly aligned with the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize external danger and vigilance, and the trigger pattern centers on assault-related cues. A dominant appraisal of losing one's mind would usually be accompanied by threat content about internal loss of control or dissociation-like danger, which is absent here.

For an assault trauma, the trigger pattern strongly suggests a sexual assault context (being naked, being looked at sexually). That is not impossible, but the rest of the profile does not support that specific context strongly enough to make the set cohere: there are no matching sexual-assault-linked threat or memory items, and the only bodily appraisal is about the body being unreliable rather than violated or contaminated.

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'I can no longer trust my own body' is more typically linked to injury, dissociation, panic-like bodily cues, or medical trauma. It does not fit well with the mainly sexual-vulnerability trigger pattern unless there is additional supporting content, which is absent here.

vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Linh

Linh was sixty-eight when it happened—a Thursday evening in late September, leaving her office building in downtown Portland after a partner meeting that had run past six. She was alone in the parking garage, heels clicking on concrete, thinking about the appellate brief due Monday, when a man stepped from behind a concrete pillar. He was younger, broader, and he had a knife. What followed was thirty-seven minutes of sexual violence in a space that smelled of motor oil and fear. He spoke very little—mostly grunts, threats delivered in a low voice close to her ear—but the sounds he made, the particular ragged quality of his breathing, the wet click of his tongue against his teeth, burned themselves into her nervous system with a permanence that surprised even her. When he left, she lay on the cold ground for what felt like hours before she could move. A security guard found her twenty minutes later.

The assault itself was reported. There was a trial, a conviction, incarceration. From the outside, Linh appeared to rebuild. She returned to her practice after six weeks. She and her husband, Robert, a retired engineer, settled into what looked like normalcy. But within months, the world had fundamentally reorganized itself around danger.

It began with sounds. A man clearing his throat in the courthouse hallway would send her heart into a gallop, her breath shortening, her palms slick. The particular timbre of a colleague's voice—something about the roughness in it—would trigger that same cascade of panic. She found herself unable to attend depositions without knowing the exact layout of the room, the location of exits, whether anyone else would be present. When opposing counsel raised his voice during a hearing, Linh's body flooded with a terror so immediate and overwhelming that she had to excuse herself. The connection was undeniable: these sounds, so similar to those burned into her memory, told her body that danger was imminent, that the threat was real and present.

Her body had become unreliable in ways that extended far beyond the courtroom. When her heart raced—and it did so constantly now, at the slightest unexpected noise, the sight of a man's silhouette, even sometimes for no discernible reason at all—she had come to believe that this racing itself was a sign of serious danger, a warning system that could not be ignored. She no longer trusted her own physiological responses to tell her the difference between genuine threat and false alarm. This distrust fed a hypervigilance that had become exhausting. She found herself scanning faces on the street, noting the way men looked at her—a glance that lingered a fraction too long, a gaze that she interpreted as sexual assessment, as predatory interest—and each time, her conviction deepened that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that she could not afford to let her guard down.

The hypervigilance, in turn, made her acutely attuned to potential triggers. She began to notice sounds everywhere: the particular rasp of a man's voice in a restaurant, the breathing pattern of someone standing too close in an elevator, the wet quality of a cough. Her nervous system had become a finely tuned threat-detection apparatus, and it was relentless. Every potential trigger reinforced her belief that she had to remain vigilant, that the world was populated with dangers she could not afford to miss. She had to be on guard all the time, because the moment she relaxed, she was convinced something terrible would happen.

At night, the fear intensified. The darkness felt less like an absence than a presence—a space where threats could hide, where her vigilance became both more necessary and less effective. She lay awake beside Robert, listening to the house settle, to sounds from the street, her heart often racing, certain that each noise carried menace. She had come to believe that safety was a daytime luxury, something that evaporated when the sun went down.

Three years have passed since the assault. Linh is seventy-one now, still practicing law, though she has quietly declined cases that would require her to work in certain buildings or neighborhoods. She has not told her colleagues why. Robert knows, but they do not discuss it. What brought her to therapy was a panic attack so severe during a client meeting that she thought she was having a heart attack—and the realization, afterward, that she could no longer function at the level her practice demanded. She is terrified that if she acknowledges how much the trauma has taken from her, she will lose what remains of her sense of control.
